description: Work out stocking density with the Grazing Stock Density Calculator — acres per head and head per acre from herd and field size. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 50 cow-calf pairs on 80 acres is a density of 1.6 acres per pair — or 0.625 pairs per acre, the same fact facing the other way.
quick_answer: The Grazing Stock Density Calculator divides a grazing area by the animals on it and reports the density both ways: acres per head and head per acre. Enter the pasture size and the herd, flock or mob count and read the density your forage, fencing and rotation decisions start from.
steps_intro: Density is the first number of grazing management — before forage, before rotation, before rain:

body.t: Rotations move a known herd through paddocks of known sizes. Density per paddock — this calculation, repeated — is the plan's skeleton.
Grazing lets are written in head per acre or acres per head. Converting the term both ways with one tool ends the negotiation's unit fog.
Headline herd sizes mislead across different acreages. Density is the comparable — the number that says which pasture is actually worked harder.

50 pairs on 80 acres: 80 ÷ 50 = 1.6 acres per pair; inversely 0.625 pairs per acre. Neither figure says whether the land can carry it — that is a forage question this density frames but does not answer.
300 ewes on 60 acres: 0.2 acres per ewe, 5 ewes per acre. Sheep numbers look startling next to cattle until the animal size enters — density is per head, and heads differ, which the FAQ covers.

faq: Stocking density from area and animal count: acres per head (area ÷ head) and head per acre (head ÷ area). Pure division, reported both ways because the industry quotes both.
Can I use the result for professional work?
As the density figure in a grazing plan, yes. Whether that density is sustainable is a forage and climate judgement — this calculator deliberately does not make it.
A standardising idea (often a 1,000 lb cow with calf) that lets mixed herds be summed. This tool counts heads as entered; convert classes to animal units first if your plan works in them.

To the land, enormously; to this division, not at all. 5 sheep per acre and 5 cattle per acre are the same density here and utterly different grazing pressure — the table's readings keep that in view.
Divide hectares by head the same way: 40 ha with 50 head is 0.8 ha per head. The Hectares to Acres Converter translates existing figures.
Stocking rate or stocking density — same thing?
Density is animals per area at a moment; rate usually folds in time (per season or year). This tool computes the instantaneous density your rotation plan schedules.
How does density change through a rotation?
It spikes in the paddock being grazed and rests at zero in the others. The whole-farm figure is the average; paddock figures are the management.
What about shared grazing with mixed stock?
Convert classes to a common animal unit before counting heads, or compute each class's density against the same acres and read them side by side.
